### Round 371 — one row per tool call

The largest remaining chat-surface divergence, closed. The reference folds a call and its result
into one `ToolCallBlock` and draws **one row per call** (`tool-call-tree.ts`,
`ToolCallTree.tsx`); native kept `tool/call` and `tool/result` as two rows, so every tool call took
two activity lines and the second carried a native-authored `Output` marker.

`reducer::rebuild` now pairs a result with its call by the wire's own identifiers — the result's
`message.toolCallId`, its `source.callId`, `role: "tool"`, and the same `turn`/`step` — the same
pairing `activity` already used for labels. A paired result folds `output` (its bounded body) and
`failed` (its exact `isError`) onto the call row and is marked `chat: false`: Chat draws the call
once, and **Trajectory still lists every record**, so the raw result is never lost. An unpaired
result keeps its own Chat row — a result that names no call is information, not a duplicate — and a
result for another step does not fold.

What the fold changed in the view: a call's expanded body is now the result it recorded (the read
body without its envelope, a bash output, an unpaired result's text), the edit call's body is still
the diff card, the failure marker reads the folded `failed` instead of the call's missing result,
and the `+N −N` totals drop on a failed call exactly as before.

transcript that replaces six), `168-tool-row-read-body.png` (a read call expanding to the two
content lines it folded), `169-tool-row-diff.png` and `170-tool-row-diff-folded.png` (the edit call's
diff and its fold). These supersede `158-…`, `163-…`, `164-…` and `166-…`, which show the two-row
shape; the numbers are kept because each is the same surface re-captured, and the older files stay
as history.

### Round 373 — the read card: a typed `meta` projection and the reference's numbered block

The first of the structured tool cards, and the one that needed data native was refusing to keep.
`readCardModel` reads the result's opaque `meta` — path, 1-based offset, numbered lines,
`totalLines`, optional `lang` — validates every field with its own rules and only then draws
`ReadBlock`; native kept `meta` private and drew the read result as text.

**The model** (`reducer/read_card.rs`) mirrors those rules rather than approximating them: the call
must be a `read` (alpha's `functions.read`/`tool-fs/read` spellings included) with a non-empty
`file_path` and only positive-integer `offset`/`limit`; the metadata's `offset` must be at least 1,
`totalLines` a non-negative integer, and its lines a strictly increasing list that begins after
`offset - 1`, never exceeds `totalLines`, with string text; the result text must be the model-facing
`<path>…<type>file</type><content>…</content>` envelope. A field that fails a rule drops the card
instead of being repaired, exactly as the reference does, and the recorded text body remains the
fallback.

**The card** draws the reference's `ReadBlock`: a toolbar row with the relativized path and, for a
windowed read, `Showing N of M lines` at its right end; numbered rows in the code face with the
gutter at the reference's `ch` width; and the same head/tail fold the primitive uses — 8 rows before
the middle collapses, 4 kept at each end, a `… N more lines` control between them. Expansion shares
the diff card's per-key state, because it is the same question.

**The pairing** is what makes it possible: `Transcript` now keeps `call seq → result seq` from the
fold round 371 added, so `activity()` reaches a call's own result in constant time instead of
scanning the tail on every frame. `summarize` delegates to a paired variant, so a caller without the
result — every existing test — keeps the old behaviour.

Evidence: `shots/172-tool-read-card.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) shows the card in the
`tool-activity-read` preset: `src/PUBLIC-note.txt`, `Showing 2 of 42 lines`, and the two numbered
lines the fixture's synthetic metadata records. The fixture now carries that metadata (it is the
shape a real session stores), so the card is drawn from data, not hard-coded.

Tests: seven in `read_card` — a complete read, a non-windowed whole file, the head/tail cap on 20
lines, six metadata failures, four envelope failures, five call/argument failures, and the `Debug`
form proving line text never leaves the model — plus the fixture's card assertions.

### Round 374 — the terminal card: exit status as result data

The second structured tool card. A shell call is the one tool family whose *failure* is not an error
flag: the bash tool settles a failing command as a completed call, `isError` stays false, and the
exit status arrives as a trailing `[exit code: N]` or `[killed by signal: X]` marker the shell
renderer appends. The reference parses that marker into a status pill and draws the command as a
terminal; native drew the whole thing as text.

**The model** (`reducer/terminal_card.rs`) follows `terminal-card-model.ts:283-341`: the call must be
`bash`/`pwsh` (alpha spellings included) with a non-empty `command`, a finite positive `timeoutMs` if
present, string `workdir` and boolean `run_in_background`. A call with no `description` is the
*persistent* shell provider, whose result has no single process status, and keeps the text body; so
does a background call, an error result, or anything that fails a rule. The workdir resolves against
the session workspace and collapses `.`/`..` segments, then labels as its last segment, `~` for home,
or the path itself. Output loses its ANSI sequences (native has no styled-run renderer) and its
status marker, and a command that printed nothing says `No output`.

**The card** draws one prompt row per command line — the first led by the resolved directory label,
later rows a bare `$`, which is the reference's own rule that the cwd labels the *call* — the status
pill at the right, and the output rows with the primitive's 16-row head/tail fold (8 + 8) behind the
same `… N more lines` control the other two cards use. The one part not drawn is the run-state dot:
the row above already carries the state, which is the primitive's `runStateDot={false}` variant.

Evidence: `shots/173-tool-terminal-card.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) in the new
`tool-activity-terminal` preset, whose bash result is recorded the way the reference records a failing
command — `isError: false`, output, then `[exit code: 2]`. The card shows `workspace`, the command,
`exit code 2`, and the two output lines; the error-marker count assertion records that this preset
carries no error flag.

Tests: eight in `terminal_card` — a clean settle with no pill, a failing command as a completed call,
a signal taking precedence, empty and escape-only output, a multi-line command, the 8/8 cap on 20
lines, the six refused cases, and the prompt label over home/relative/absolute workdirs — plus the
preset's card assertions, and one that proves neither card prints its content through `Debug`.

### Round 375 — the search card: a grep's grouped matches and a glob's paths

The third structured tool card. `grep` and `glob` carry their own result shape in `meta` — matches
grouped by file, or a flat path list — plus `total` (what the search found) and `truncated`
(whether the page was capped). The reference treats the pair as one card whose banner states both
numbers so a capped page cannot read as a complete one, and native drew it as text.

**The model** (`reducer/search_card.rs`) follows `search-card-model.ts:78-100`: `grep`/`glob` (alpha
spellings included) with `pattern` (non-empty for grep, non-blank for glob), an optional non-blank
`path`, and for grep an `include` that is neither empty, negated, nor comma-separated outside braces
— the tool's own alternation syntax, so `*.{rs,md}` stays valid and `*.rs,*.md` does not. `meta`
must carry a boolean `truncated`, an integer `total`, and the shape matching the tool: `matches`
with per-file `lineNumber` (1-based) and string `line`, or `paths` of strings. A rule that fails
keeps the text body.

**The card** draws the reference's banner (`3 matches · 2 files`, or `Showing 3 of 120 matches · 2
files`; `2 paths` / `Showing 1 of 90 paths`), then the flattened rows — a file header carrying the
path and its retained count, each match as `N: line`, or one path per row — capped at 8 with the
head/tail fold behind `… N more results`. An empty result says `No results`.

### Round 377 — the ask-user transcript: questions paired with what was chosen

The fifth structured tool card, and the one whose data is the user's own words. An
`ask_user_question` call records its questions in the arguments; the result records the answers,
both as JSON keyed by stable ids. The reference pairs them and draws each question with what was
chosen — or names the verdict when the set never took answers — and native drew the raw record.

**The model** (`reducer/ask_card.rs`) follows `ask-question-row.tsx:95-170`: the call must be
`ask_user_question` with a non-empty `questions` array of unique string ids, string `question`,
optional string `header`/`detail`, an array `options` and a boolean `multi_select`. The result text
must parse as `{answers: [{id, selected: [string], custom?}]}`, and the pairing is exact — a
different count, a repeated id, or an id that was never asked yields **no card**, because a partial
pairing would show answers under the wrong questions. An empty `custom` string is not an answer.
A failed call with `error.code` `ASK_CANCELLED` or `ASK_ABORTED` draws the verdict (`cancelled`,
`interrupted`) and the question list instead; any other failure stays a tool error.

**The card** states the reference's summary — `1/2 answered`, or the verdict — as its banner, then

### Round 378 — the applied diff, and the editor's own shape

Two gaps in the diff card's *derivation*, both visible on a real session.

**A settled mutation was drawing the intended change, not the change.** The reference prefers the
diff the Host recorded as applied (`meta.diffs`) and falls back to the intended one only for a
`write` (`diff-card-model.ts:71-104`). Native always drew the intended one, so a `write` that
overwrote a different previous content, or an `edit` whose applied result differed from its
arguments, showed a diff the session never had. `Transcript::activity` now takes the applied list
when the call is settled: exactly one hunk replaces the card, an empty list keeps a `write`'s
whole-file diff and drops an `edit`'s, and a malformed list invalidates the whole thing rather than
being skipped. A **multi-file** applied result keeps the intended diff, because this card draws one
file and showing the first would misrepresent the rest — a deliberate difference, recorded here.

**A `str_replace_editor` was invisible.** The Anthropic-style editor names the same mutation with
`command`/`path`/`file_text`/`old_str`/`new_str`; the reference derives its diff from those while it
runs and draws **no** card once settled. Native recognised the tool nowhere. It now maps to its own
verb, derives the intended diff for `create` and `str_replace` while running, and drops the card on
settle — the reference's rule, pinned by a test that asserts both halves.

Evidence: `shots/177-tool-applied-diff.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) in the new
`tool-activity-applied` preset, whose edit result records `newText: "PUBLIC applied text"` while the
call's arguments say "PUBLIC new text": the card draws the applied line.

Tests: `applied_tests` (the editor's two commands and its refusals, the strict narrowing, `file()`),
and `settled_diff_tests` (applied replaces intended, the no-op write and edit rules, the editor's
running/settled pair, and the multi-file fallback).

### Round 379 — the cards' Copy control

Every reference card that carries a `CodeToolbar` has a **Copy** control that copies the raw recorded
text — not the card's chrome, not the parsed rows — and reads `Copied` for a second. Native's cards
had none, so a read, a terminal's output or a search's matches could be examined but not taken.

`Message::CopyCard` copies the row's folded result body through the same `write_clipboard` path the
settings fields use (the Wayland-safe worker write, or iced's own on a non-Wayland session), sets a
one-second `Copied` state with a `Task::perform` timer that clears it, and is drawn in the three
places the reference draws it: the read card's toolbar beside the window status, the terminal card's
header beside the exit pill, and the search card's banner at the row's right end. The button is
absent when the row recorded no text, because a copy control with nothing to copy is a lie.

### Round 381 — the model-retry row

Round 380 corrected an index line by claiming native "states the retry in its own retry row". It did
not: native had no retry row at all, and `llm/retry` fell through the generic branch into a
Trajectory-only JSON line. This round builds the row the claim assumed.

**The model** (`reducer/retry_ui.rs`) follows the session format's own validation
(`payload-validation.ts:119-138`): `mode` is `normal` (which requires `maxRetries`, and `retry` may
not exceed it) or `always` (which must omit it); `retry` is at least 1; `delayMs` is a non-negative
integer inside the timer range; `provider` and `policyKey` are non-empty. The failure's message is
the reason the row states. `State` holds the chain's attempts plus the started receipts, and derives
the reference's copy: `Waiting to retry model request (2/3) · 4s` while scheduled, `Retried model
request (2/3)` once a receipt arrives, `Model request retry cancelled (1/3)` when the owning turn
closed first; `always` mode omits the ceiling.

**The row** is one per chain, not one per event (`retry.ts:76-100`): the first `llm/retry` opens it,
later attempts and `llm/retry-started` receipts patch it, and a `turn/end` or `step/end` cancels a
still-scheduled attempt. It draws as an unboxed line — a clock glyph, the state line, then the
recorded `Retry delay: 4s` and `Failure reason: …` beneath it. Every record stays in Trajectory, so
nothing is lost.

Evidence: `shots/181-model-retry.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) in the new `model-retry`
preset: one attempt started, one waiting out 4 seconds, with its reason.

ceiling, a started attempt, a cancelled one, and the format's payload rules) and four in
`retry_row_tests` (one row per chain patched by later attempts, the started receipt, the close
cancelling a scheduled attempt, and a payload the format rejects contributing nothing).

### Round 382 — the retry countdown is live

Round 381's row stated the recorded delay as a constant, so a waiting attempt read "· 4s" forever.
The reference counts down (`retrySeconds` = `max(1, ceil(ms/1000))`, re-read on a one-second
timer), anchoring the deadline to its **first render** rather than to the Host's event clock,
because a browser may sit on another machine with another clock (`MessageItem.tsx:41-69`).

Native now does the same: the app anchors each retry row the first time a frame carries it
(`retry_anchored`, in this machine's milliseconds), derives `remaining = delay − (now − anchor)`
with the reference's ceiling and its never-below-one rule, and ticks once a second — but only while
a visible row is *scheduled*, so a started or cancelled chain costs no timer. The fixture proves it
on its own: `shots/182-model-retry-countdown.png` was grabbed about a second after the frame
applied, and the row reads `· 3s` where round 381's showed `· 4s`.

started/cancelled chain having none, and the parsed-payload path) and `retry_countdown_ui_tests` (the
anchor is taken once and survives later frames, the row states its own delay rather than the fixture's

reference), and draws inline and display math as code-styled source. No native typesetter exists, so
"show the source in code" is the honest rendering — the reference maps both to KaTeX — and that is
recorded in the table's renderer row rather than left implicit.

claim, but a chat image is a text placeholder (`reducer.rs:1315`) with no decode path and a fetch

statistics dialog — all built this session — had no row at all; they do now. The process-group and

### Round 388 — the created-task card for `schedule_create`

Round 387 corrected the index's claim about creating schedules, and the truth pointed at a missing
card rather than a missing form: neither client has a create form — the reference creates tasks
through the **`schedule_create`** tool and renders the created task as its own transcript card
(`schedule-create-card.ts:135-152`, `ScheduleCreateCard.tsx:36-110`). Native had the generic tool
row.

**The card** (`reducer/schedule_card.rs`) reads the task from the tool's result — its canonical
value serialized as JSON — and narrows every field: a non-empty `id`, `prompt` and `scheduledAt`, a
known `kind`, and that kind's own fields (`afterSeconds`, `everySeconds`, `time`/`timeZone`,
`weekdays` of ISO 1–7, `expression`). The title is the recorded `title`, else the instruction's first
line. The rule line follows the reference's wording — `Once`, `Every 5 minutes` (the largest unit that
divides the interval), `Daily at 17:30 (UTC)`, `Weekly on Mon, Fri at 09:00 (UTC)`,
`Cron 0 9 * * 1 (UTC)` — with one recorded difference: the zone is the raw IANA id where the reference
prints an offset plus its locale's long name (`schedule-format.ts:135-146`), because native has no ICU
zone names.

A running call already states the title it is preparing from its own arguments; a failed creation or
a result that is not a complete task states the raw result text instead, so the card never presents
an identity it does not have — which is the reference's own rule.

`schedule-create` preset: the row reads `Scheduled task · PUBLIC weekly fixture reminder` and the
card `◷ PUBLIC weekly fixture reminder` over `Weekly on Mon, Fri at 09:00 (UTC)`.

### Round 391 — a manual compaction's single marker, and a row that drew nothing

The reference folds a manual `/compact` and the compaction it produced into **one** marker: titled
`compact`, its summary the structured counts (`Compacted 5 history items (~2.4k tokens)`), expandable
to the summary — with the command's own text only as the fallback when no counts exist
(`CompactionCommandCard.tsx:14-26`, `CompactionItem.tsx:56-66`). Round 390's command row had left
this as *two* rows: the command and a separate `Context summarized` row.

**The fold** now reads the compaction summary the command's `sourceEventSeq` cites, attaches its
`shadowedSeqs` count and `shadowedTokenCount` to the command row, and marks that summary row
Chat-invisible (`Trajectory` still lists it). A `/compact` states `Compacting context…` while
running, the counts once settled, and its own outcome text when no summary exists.

**A row that drew nothing.** The first capture of this marker was an empty frame: the row reserved
its height and its branch ran (proved by a temporary print, since removed), yet no ink appeared. The
cause was the row's spacer — `Space::new().width(Length::Fill)` keeps a `Fill` *height*, which
collapses a shrink-to-fit `Row` to zero height. The row is now one label carrying the whole line
(the chevron, the command's name, the summary) with its output lines below it, which paints, and the
expanded body's height is reserved from the same line count the render draws (capped at ten). I first
tried splitting the disabled-button arm from a plain container and the spacer fix alone; neither
changed a pixel, which is why the row was rewritten rather than patched again. Shot 190 was re-taken
because the row's markup changed.

### Round 395 — the process-group seat closes

### Round 399 — the work-details policy the reference selects from

The reference's grouping behaviour is not fixed: a persisted **Work details** preference selects one
of four modes — Compact, Standard, Detailed, Verbose — and each mode enables a policy table:

`settledReasoningPreview` (`presentation-policy.ts:11-56`, `settings/TranscriptViewRow.tsx`,
`locale.ts:295-301`). The default is Standard.

This round lands that table as `app/src/work_details.rs` — the four modes with the reference's exact
policy values, their labels and persisted keys, and the two derived questions a renderer asks
(`groups(settled)` and `starts_folded(settled)`). The process seat now reads the **default** mode's
policy rather than a hardcoded rule, so native's current behaviour is exactly Standard: groups on
every turn, a settled turn folded, a live one open — **corrected in round 512**: the reference's
seat starts folded while the turn runs too, so a grouped seat is folded until the reader opens it.

What is deliberately not built yet: the Settings row that chooses a mode. It needs a persisted
preference, and a control that forgets on restart would be a defect rather than a feature, so the row
and its storage land together in the next round.

Two wiring lessons from this one: a module shared by `ui.rs` must be declared *inside* `ui.rs` (with
`#[path]`), because the smoke examples compile `ui` without the binary's module list; and a `mod`
declared in both roots is a duplicate definition, not a convenience.

The composer audit's first absent item was the reference's second `/` source: skills. Its remote call

(`session-controller/lib/typert.remote-client.d.ts:62`, `types.ts:263-284`) — returning
`{ skills: SkillEntry[] }` with `name`, `description`, optional `whenToUse` and `modelInvocable`.

commands already do), `Endpoint::SkillsList`, and `NativeClient::skills_list`, which sends the
reference's object shape and refuses only a catalog that cannot be addressed — more than 512 entries

documented at the call site: commands take a flat `agentId`, skills take the request object, because
those are the two shapes the reference's own typings declare.

table now says exactly that instead of listing "skills in the slash menu" as absent.

### Round 421 — schedule instants read as local time

The schedules rows and delivery records printed the Host's stored instants verbatim —
`2026-10-17T09:00:00Z` — where the reference converts them (`schedule-format.ts:321-334`) and pairs
the next run with a relative form (`list.nextPrefix`).

`time_text` now owns that conversion without a new dependency: `parse_instant` reads RFC 3339 with a
`Z` or explicit offset (fixed-width fields only, so `2026-1-1` and `+2:00` are refused rather than
guessed), `local_date_time` asks the platform for the local zone through the same thread-safe
`localtime_r` the chat clock uses, and `relative` states `in 2 hours` / `3 days overdue` / `now`. A
stored value that cannot be read keeps its original text on screen, which is the only honest fallback.

The rows now read `Daily at 09:00 (UTC) · Enabled · next run 2026-10-17 04:00 (1 day overdue)`,
`Last delivered 2026-10-16 04:00`, and the history pair `2026-10-16 04:00 → 2026-10-16 04:00`.

Evidence: `shots/236-schedule-local-times.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) in the
`schedules-history` preset — the converted next run with its relative form, the local delivery stamp
and the local history pair.

Tests: three in `time_text` — epoch vectors computed independently (including both offset spellings
equalling `Z`), eight malformed instants refused with the stored text kept, and the relative form's
coarse and signed shapes.

### Round 430 — full access cannot be enabled from Settings on one press

A settings audit found a real safety gap, and a doc claim that said it was already closed. Settings →
General's "Permission for new sessions" row wrote whatever preset was chosen — including Full access,
the deployment-wide default for every new session — with no confirmation. The reference never does
(`PermissionRow.tsx:81-87,105-125`): choosing Full access opens a risk confirmation with an
acknowledgement, an Enable button that stays inert until it is ticked, and Cancel; the copy is
`confirm.title` / `confirm.description` / `confirm.acknowledge` / `confirm.enable` / `confirm.cancel`.

Native now behaves the same, and the guard lives in the model rather than in one caller: `handle`
refuses any `PermissionDefault` naming a full-access preset until the acknowledgement is ticked, and
refuses a confirmation that does not match the pending choice or that has not been acknowledged. The
row's preset list closes while the confirmation is open, so a second choice cannot slip past it.

The coverage text that claimed the guard already covered the settings row cited the reference's settings
row while describing the composer's picker; it now says which surfaces carry it.

Evidence: `shots/245-full-access-confirm.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) in the new
`settings-full-access` preset — the confirmation inside the General page, the already-disabled Enable
button, and Cancel beside it.

Tests: three in `settings_tests` — arming writes nothing and an unacknowledged Enable is refused; a
non-full-access choice is not guarded and Cancel leaves nothing behind; and the spellings
(`full-access`, `danger-full-access`, case and underscore variants) are all recognised.

### Round 440 — a job's stop confirmation expires

The reference arms its stop control for three seconds and lets it fall back to idle
(`JobListAction.tsx:52-56,423-430`, with a test asserting the fallback). Native armed it until the user
pressed again or armed another row, so an armed `✕` and its refusal line could survive indefinitely —
and a stray press much later would have sent a `job/kill` the user no longer meant.

Arming now schedules `Message::JobArmExpired` for three seconds; the message disarms only the row it
was armed for, so arming a second row cannot be cancelled by the first row's timer.

Three rounds recorded "no frame" for the jobs panel. The cause was not the panel, the header or the
layout: it was where the preset's seed ran. The `jobs-panel` block had been inserted inside the
**settings** arm of `build`'s preset match, so for a conversation preset it never executed at all —
`header_crumbs` saw `jobs = 0` and drew only the title. A temporary `eprintln!` in `header_crumbs`
settled it in one run (`jobs=0` for a plain conversation, `jobs=4` once the seed moved to the end of
`build`), which is the check that should have come before the third capture attempt rather than after
it.

With the seed last, the frame shows what the earlier rounds' code produces: the header crumb
`2 background jobs running`, the panel's `Running` section with the shell job expanded to its output,
`Build the release binary` mid-stop, the `Finished 2` section with `Search for parity notes` and
`Lint the app crate` (red), the armed `Stop task Run the test suite` / `Click again to confirm`
confirmation — and, from round 438, a stop control on the **running** row only.

**The frame was visually verified but its report was not `status: passed`** in that round, because
`expectedControlCountsMatch` compared the drawn controls against a metadata flag that said "every
non-modal preset draws a stop control". The flag was the wrong predicate: the composer draws a stop
only while the session runs. It is fixed in the next round, and the frame is archived as passed
`shots/253-jobs-panel.png`.

### Round 451 — the transport keeps the producer's job facts

Every remaining jobs gap came down to one cause: native's `JobView` kept five fields and dropped
everything else the Host sends. The producer's `JobView` carries `progress`, `detail`, `startedAt`,
`finishedAt` and the output ring's `total`/`earliest`/`spillPaths`
(`packages/jobs/jobs/src/view.ts:65-102`), and the four unbuilt panel behaviours all read from them.

The DTO now carries all of it: `progress` and `detail` as optional strings, `startedAt`/`finishedAt`
as optional epoch millis with the Host's own camelCase names, and `output` as an optional
`JobOutput { total, earliest, spill_paths }`. Nothing is invented when the Host omits a field — a live
job has no `finished_at` and no `detail`, and a deployment that sends no ring leaves `output: None`
rather than a zeroed struct pretending to be measured.

Tests: three in `transport::dto::job_view_tests` — a full frame keeps every producer fact, the minimal
live frame parses with the absences intact, and serializing a sparse row writes none of the omitted
keys.

This is wire work without a frame; the panel's ordering, progress text, duration cell and
expand-when-observable behaviours are the next rounds, each with its own capture.

### Round 453 — a job row states how long it has run

The reference's rows carry a duration cell: elapsed to now while live, start to finish once settled,
in three forms — hours and minutes past an hour, minutes and seconds past a minute, seconds below that
(`JobListAction.tsx:116-124,193-202`, `locales.ts:70-72`).

`job_list::duration` renders those three forms, and the row draws the cell at its right edge before the
stop control, measured at render time so a live job's number is current. A clock that moved backwards
reads as `0s`, never a negative span, and a job with no start instant gets no cell at all rather than a
fabricated one.

### Round 460 — typing into the terminal reaches the shell

The largest terminal gap: the reference pipes its terminal's key handler straight to the Host
(`ui-sidebar-terminal/src/client/terminal.tsx:101,138`), so Enter, arrows, Escape and Ctrl combinations
reach the shell. Native had a single-line field and a Write button, so a typed command arrived
unterminated and Ctrl-C was impossible.

Two pieces, both tested:

1. `terminal_keys::bytes` maps a key press to the bytes it stands for — named keys to their escape
   sequences, Ctrl+letter to its control byte, a printable character as itself, and **nothing** for a
   key the table does not name.
2. `Action::Key` sends those bytes through the same guarded write path the button uses: it refuses when
   another attachment holds control, when the panel is detached, while any operation is outstanding, and
   over the Host's byte bound. It never edits the typed line, because the reference's terminal has no
   line for a key to land in.

The panel owns the keyboard while open: `key_pressed` diverts a mapped key to the terminal and lets
everything it does not name fall through, so Escape and the app's shortcuts still work.

Tests: `terminal_keys` (named keys, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D as control bytes, an unmapped key sending
nothing) and `a_key_sends_its_bytes_without_touching_the_typed_line` (one write, the field untouched, an
empty keystroke sending nothing).

The test caught a real bug before the frame ever existed: the first Ctrl mapping formatted the control
byte as a decimal string, which would have sent the literal characters "3" to the shell for Ctrl-C.

**Recorded limit**: this is a key-to-bytes translation, not an emulator. The screen is still the
sanitized text panel recorded in `FEATURE-PARITY.md:22`, so a full-screen TUI will not render — but its
keys, including Ctrl-C, now reach the process.

### Round 461 — the terminal remembers which shell you chose

The reference remembers the shell a user picked in a preference key and re-selects it on the next visit,
falling back to the first discovered only when the Host no longer offers it
(`api/terminal-controller/src/client/shell-preference.ts:2`, `model.ts:125-129`). Native reset the
selection on every open and defaulted to index 0, so a user with several shells was returned to the
first every time.

The panel now keeps the chosen shell **by path**, not by index: a new `loaded` reply looks the remembered
path up in the Host's fresh list, selects it wherever it now sits, and only then falls back to the first
entry. A Host that reorders its shells therefore still opens the one the user chose.

Tests: `the_chosen_shell_is_remembered_across_opens` — a second shell is chosen, the panel is reopened,
and the Host's next reply lists them in the opposite order; the remembered shell is still selected, which
a stored index could not have produced.

**Recorded difference**: the reference persists this in the browser's localStorage, so it survives a
reload; native remembers it for the life of the process. Persisting it in the app's own layout document
is the follow-up, and it is recorded here rather than implied.

### Round 462 — the chosen shell survives a restart

Round 461 remembered the shell for the life of the process and recorded the difference: the reference
stores it in a preference key, so a reload keeps it. That difference is closed.

The layout document gains `layout.terminalShell`, holding the path — not an index, which would silently
point at a different shell when the Host reorders its list. `parse_terminal_shell` accepts only what
looks like a path: absolute, non-empty, bounded to the namespace's own 4096 bytes, and free of control
characters, so a corrupted entry leaves the panel on the Host's first shell instead of building a
create review around nonsense. The stored value is adopted before the panel ever opens, and choosing a
shell writes it through the same layout store the other General preferences use.

Tests: `only_an_absolute_bounded_path_is_stored` — accepted paths, a trimmed one, and rejections for the
empty string, a relative path, a control character and an over-long value; the panel's own
`the_chosen_shell_is_remembered_across_opens` still covers selecting by path after a reorder.

### Round 467 — the catalog opens on hover, after the reference's delay

The subagent audit's seventh difference: the reference opens the catalog when the pointer rests on the
trigger for 150ms and closes it 120ms after the pointer leaves, with a click pinning it open
(`SubagentHeaderLineage.tsx:520-538`). Native required a click, so reaching the tree meant moving to a
control that a pointer-driven user would expect to open.

The trigger is now a `mouse_area`: entering arms `Message::SubagentHover(true)`, which schedules
`SubagentHoverExpired` after 150ms, and that message opens the catalog only if the pointer is *still*
there and nothing is open. The delay is the point — a cursor crossing the header must not open a popup —
and a click still works exactly as before.

Tests: `hovering_the_subagent_trigger_opens_it_only_after_the_delay` — entering opens nothing, the
elapsed delay opens it, and a delay that fires after the pointer left changes nothing.

**Recorded difference**: the reference also *closes* 120ms after the pointer leaves. Native keeps the
catalog open until a click, Escape or an outside press, because a popup that vanishes while the user is
moving toward it is the failure a hover-close usually produces; the behaviour is named here rather than
copied blindly.

### Round 488 — a failed upload offers its own retry

The composer audit's third finding: the reference states `Upload failed; click to retry` on the card and
carries a retry control (`locales.ts:73-74`, `FileCard.tsx:38-71`), while native said `Not staged · no
Host metadata` and offered only Remove — so a transient failure cost a full re-pick through the path
field or the picker.

`Draft` now keeps the path it staged, a rejection records whether a retry is honest, and `Draft::retry`
re-stages the same file with a fresh ticket without asking for the path again. The card states
`Upload failed · retry or remove` and the notice says `Upload failed; retry or choose the file again.`

**Not every rejection is retryable, and the code says which**: a transport that did not send is; an intake
rejection (too large, not a regular file, unavailable, invalid path) is not, because the same file would
fail the same way — the reference's retry control exists only for the upload state, and the test pins the
distinction.

**Recorded**: the reference also draws a byte progress bar from `progress` (`FileCard.tsx:74-79`). Native's
stage command is one request with no progress reporting, so there is nothing honest to draw; the card says
`Uploading…` and the bar is named here rather than faked.

Tests: `a_failed_upload_retries_the_same_file_and_an_intake_rejection_does_not` — a not-sent upload is
retryable and its retry mints a new ticket for the same slot, while a too-large rejection is not
retryable and refuses.

Evidence: `shots/275-file-failed.png` (DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`) — `Upload failed / retry or
remove` with its Retry control and the notice line.

### Round 502 — the user bubble draws its own 22px line

`reference.png` is in the workspace root at last: the user's own 1980x1319 capture was already on
disk in `~/Pictures/Screenshots/`, hashes to the expected `b8e164f5...`, and is now copied to the
documented path — so the comparison that had been blocked since round 1 ran.

**What it proved.** The reference's `.bubble` sets `line-height: calc(22px + var(--dsh-content-font-delta, 0px))`
(`ui-chat/src/client/chat/MessageItem.module.css:38`), and the sheet's own comment states the
contract: "42px single-line bubble at the default size: 22 line + 10 vertical padding each side".
Measured in the reference: four bubble lines at y 357/379/401/423 — **22px** apart — while the
assistant lines under them are 24px apart (572 -> 596). Native measured *and* drew both rows at the
shared 24px body box, 2px per line too tall.

**The fix, in both halves.** `design::BUBBLE_LINE` (22) and `bubble_line(delta)` beside
`LINE_BODY`/`body_line`; `chat_geometry`'s human path measures at that line and floors/caps the body
at it; the human body's `plain_view` draws the same line, so a wrapped bubble cannot clip.

**Measured after** (`shots/296-bubble-line.png`, DP-2 alongside, `status: passed`, mode
`tool-activity`, 1980x1319): bubble lines 135 -> 157 = **22**, and the bubble fill is 121..184 =
**64px** = 2 x 22 + 10/10. The reference's four-line bubble is 108 = 4 x 22 + 20, so the two agree
line for line. Assistant rows stay at 24.

Tests: `a_single_line_bubble_draws_the_bubbles_own_twenty_two_pixel_line` — one line reserves the
bubble's 22, four lines cap at 4 x 22, a +3 content delta moves the bubble's line to 25 while the
assistant's goes to 27, and 22 + the 10/10 `USER_BUBBLE_PAD` is the sheet's 42. The three existing
expectations that had encoded 24 for a human row (`same_key_hits...`, `unicode_newlines...`,
`measured_chat_heights...`) now name `BUBBLE_LINE` and say why.

**Recorded, not silently fixed**, from the same comparison: the message rows still carry a 14px
horizontal pad the reference does not (reference text at lane +1, native at lane +19) — **closed in
round 504**, where both insets were removed and every row measured at lane +0/+1 — and the
reference is a different state — collapsed sidebar rail, lane centred 33px right of the window
centre, scrolled transcript with no header — so a pixel-level diff needs a matching-state preset
before any 1-to-1 claim.

### Round 503 — the header counts the open session's reminders

**The gap.** The reference registers an icon-only clock chip in the Conversation header's utilities
slot: `order: -5`, left of the overflow menu and right of the leading utilities
(`ui-schedule/src/client/index.ts:208-230`). Its accessible name is the count —
`{count} reminder` / `{count} reminders` / `Reminders` (`locales.ts:42-43` `trigger.one`,
`trigger.other`, `trigger.label`) — and it opens a 336px popover of the Session's active tasks with
each row's rule, next run and a per-row delete, plus a loading line and a failure with Retry
(`ScheduleCatalogAction.tsx:35-200`, `ScheduleCatalogAction.module.css:1-189`). Native had no entry
at all: the sidebar's Scheduled tasks row was the only way to reach the catalog. Rounds 501 and 502
recorded it as still open.

**What native does now.** `reminders_action` draws the chip in the same place — the utilities cluster
right of the free space, immediately left of `More ▾` — and `reminders_menu_view` the popover under
it. The count comes from the Host's whole `schedule/catalog`, filtered to the open Session's
still-active rows (`schedule_card::is_open_reminder`), because that read is the one schedule route
native owns; the reference's header instead issues a per-Session `schedule/list`
(`session-schedule-state.ts:31-41`), and its Sidebar marks project the same filter onto the same
whole catalog (`:73-82`). Rows are ordered overdue first, then by next run, keeping catalog order on
ties (`schedule_card::order_reminders`, mirroring `schedule-format.ts:442-458`), and an overdue row
takes the reference's warning surface and label ink (`ScheduleCatalogAction.module.css:82-88,147-149`).

**Deliberate differences, each with its reason.**

1. **The chip states its count** (`◷ 2 reminders`) where the web draws a bare 16px clock and puts the
   count only in the accessible name. Native's accessibility tree publishes a fixed vocabulary of
   composer controls (`app/src/accessibility.rs:295-335`), so an icon-only chip would reach assistive
   technology as nothing; the subagent chip already states its count the same way. `◷` is the
   schedule glyph the created-task card draws.
2. **A row's name opens the schedules page**, where the reference opens the task in its right Sidebar
   (`ScheduleCatalogAction.tsx:198`); native's right Sidebar is the recorded full-page-details
   difference, and the page is the one place a task has a detail view.
3. **Delete asks first, in the row** (`Delete this reminder and its saved delivery records?` then
   `Delete reminder` / `Cancel`), where the reference's trash deletes at once and confirms through a
   shell toast (`DeleteToast.tsx:80-87`). The repo's rule is that a destructive action keeps a visible
   confirmation and its button names what it persists; native has no toast overlay, so the popover
   states the outcome itself and calls the deleted thing a *reminder* where the page says *task*.
4. **`design::WARN_SURFACE`** (`#2a251d`) is a new palette entry. The web's overdue surface is the
   flat, warm `--dsw-alias-state-warn-tertiary` = `rgb(39, 36, 31)` (`design-platform.css:377`);
   Rosé Pine's dark surfaces are cool, so no tint of `GOLD` reaches it. The first attempt used
   `GOLD` at alpha `0.08`, and the frame showed a heavy brown — Iced composites in linear space, so
   the alpha behaved like ~0.24 in sRGB. The frame caught it; the solid constant replaced it.

**The read contract, and the tests it changed.** The catalog is now read once when the transport
becomes ready, through `request_reminders` with the same gates as `request_catalog` (no smoke
profile, no fixture background reads, ready, not stopped, no observations lost, not closing, no read
in flight). Opening the tasks page, its Refresh, and native's own deletes and updates read it again,
as before. The web re-reads per header mount and on `schedule/changed`; the missing live refresh is
the already-recorded gap, so a task created or delivered while the app runs reaches the chip only on
the next read.

That makes **two** automatic startup reads, so the nine test sites that asserted "the startup catalog
is the only automatic read" now name the second one. Their point is unchanged — no auth, settings or
model-selection call joins them.

**A mistake inside this round.** The read was first placed in `choose` (then at `Event::Selected`),
the moment a Session opens, which reads closer to the reference's mount. Five tests that assert the
command order after a selection failed, and after moving it to the selected-snapshot branch,
**41** strict queue tests failed, including `presets_render_actual_app_without_queued_effects`. The
snapshot branch fires in almost every unit test, so that placement turned a startup read into a
per-test side effect. The ready-time read is the placement the repository already sanctions.

**Tests.** `the_header_chip_counts_only_the_open_sessions_active_reminders` (a same-session inactive
row and another session's live row are both excluded, and the status compare is the page's),
`an_overdue_reminder_is_listed_before_a_later_one` (overdue leads despite a later target, an undated
row sorts last, equal targets keep catalog order), `one_reminder_says_one_and_two_say_two` (singular

(the fixture preset: two live rows, the absent chip for an empty session, the chip kept for a failed

### Round 504 — message rows sit flush with the lane

**The gap.** Round 502 closed the bubble's 22px line and measured the next one from the same
reference frame: "the message rows still carry a 14px horizontal pad the reference does not
(reference text at lane +1, native at lane +19)". Reading the reference's sheets shows the rows
carry no horizontal inset at all — `.column` is the only horizontal box chat rows live in
(`ChatView.module.css:54-59`), the assistant body adds none (`AssistantMarkdown.module.css:9-18`,
`.root`/`.body`), `.userRow` adds none and only `.bubble` pads its own text (`MessageItem.module.css:3-40`),
and every unboxed row states zero horizontal padding (`.retryRow`/`.retrySummary`,
`.turnErrorRow`; `ChatGroupSeat.module.css:1-20`; `ToolRow.module.css:10-24`).

Native had **two** insets, not one: an 8px outer row padding and a 28px body inset
(`chat_geometry::BODY_INSET`, two 14px halves) for 18px total — measured at lane +18/+19 for
assistant text, the thoughts line, the process seat and the tool rows, and the user bubble's right
edge 7px inside the lane. The `8` was not an independent bug: `geometry.width` was computed as
`lane - 8` for assistant, tool and unknown rows, so the padding and the measurement agreed on the
wrong model.

**The change, in measurement and rendering together.** The outer row padding is 0; `BODY_INSET` is
`0.0`; `geometry.width` is the lane itself for assistant, tool and unknown rows, and the human cap is
`lane.min(0.702 * lane, 0.82 * lane)` with no outer subtraction. The unboxed rows that still carried
14px (retry, turn-failure notice) and 8px (the tool row's button) are zeroed, as is the process
seat's 14px. `MIN_LANE` stays 47 — its derivation, "the 0.702 share must cover the 32px bubble inset
plus one pixel of body", is unchanged — while `MALFORMED_LANE` drops from 104 to 96 because its old
comment was "outer 8 + ordinary minimum bubble 96". Boxed surfaces keep their inner padding: the
turn-trigger card is the web's `padding: 12px 16px` (`TurnTriggerNodeView.module.css:14`), the
command row is `GenericCommandCard`'s `12px 16px`, and the bubble keeps its own `10px 16px`.

**Measured, before -> after** (the `chat-transcript` preset at the reference's 1980x1319; lane
x 660..1580 from the fixture's width handles):

1. thoughts line: 678 -> **660**
2. assistant text: 679 -> **661**
3. assistant action row: 686 -> **668** (the reference's own 8px `margin-left`,
   `MessageIconActions.module.css:35`, unchanged)
4. process seat: 675 -> **661**
5. tool result row: 695 -> **683** (first ink after its 16px leading box)

The reference frame puts its own first ink at lane +1 as well (measured 565 against a lane left of
563-564), so the two now agree within a pixel on the horizontal axis. The user bubble's fill ends at
1577 where the lane ends at 1580 — the 3px is its 1px stroke plus antialiasing — so it is flush,
as `.userRow { align-items: flex-end }` inside an unpadded column is.

**Tests.** `a_message_row_spans_the_whole_lane_without_a_horizontal_inset` pins the new rule: the
assistant and tool rows measure the lane itself, `BODY_INSET` is zero (the view draws bodies at
`width - BODY_INSET`, so a non-zero inset would leave a flush row's body short), and the bubble is
measured at the lane's 0.702 share rather than a lane less an outer inset. Five existing geometry
expectations that encoded `lane - 8` were re-derived, not loosened: 842 -> 850, 1192 -> 1200,
592 -> 600, 692 -> 700 (both tool and unknown roles) and 992 -> 1000 (assistant and interrupted
assistant), plus the narrow-lane 132 -> 140.

**Mistakes inside this round.**

1. I first changed `MIN_LANE` to 33 by re-deriving it from the removed 8px. That was wrong — 47 comes
   from the 0.702 share covering the 32px bubble inset plus one pixel, which the 8px never entered —
   and the malformed-extreme-widths test caught it (`geometry.width >= 32.0` failed at a 33px lane
   whose 0.702 share is 23px). Reverted to 47.
2. The first pass zeroed only the message rows and the outer inset, and the recapture showed the tool
   row still 4px inside: the seat and the tool row own their own insets in different modules. The
   frame, not the suite, caught that they belonged to the same family.

**Still different, and named.** The vertical rhythm is untouched: native still draws a 10px body
padding and flow gaps where the reference's spacing is entirely flow margins, so a vertical
comparison needs its own round — **closed in round 510**, where the padding and the assistant
footer's gap were replaced by the reference's flow margins and 16px footer offset. The reference
frame remains a different state (cropped/scrolled), so no pixel-level 1-to-1 claim follows from
this one.

instead draws stacked `splitLine` rows of two `.cell`s (`FileDiff.tsx:176-254`,
`FileDiff.module.css:6-22`). Native had the wrap toggle and one column; the split layout was a named
deliberate second layout that did not exist.

**What native does now.** `inline_diff::split_rows` pairs each run of deletions with the additions that
follow it, row by row, keeps a context line on both sides with each side's own number, leaves the
shorter side's trailing rows empty, and gives a header or fold a `full` row across both columns
(`FileDiff.tsx:79-104`). `one_sided` says a created or deleted file has nothing to pair, so the control
is not offered and the panel stays in one column, as the reference's `split && !oneSided` does. The
panel's body draws `diff_split_row` — number gutter, colour bar, clipped (or, with wrap on, half-width
wrapped) text per side, the reference's hairline between them — and `diff_split_full` for a hunk header
(`padding: 4px 16px`, `FileDiff.module.css:14`). The toolbar gains a `Split`/`Unified` word control with
the reference's action wording; like its Wrap neighbour it is a word rather than the web's icon, which
is the recorded icon/accessibility difference.

**Deliberate differences.**

1. The reference seeds a review tab **split and unwrapped**; native keeps its wrapped, unified default
   (the user's stated preference) and offers the same toggle. `changes-split` exists to capture the
   reference's first layout, not to change native's default.
2. Each reference column is its own horizontally scrolling pane, mirrored to its peer so both sides
   move together (`FileDiff.tsx:183-200`). Native's unwrapped split cells clip at their own half and
   have no horizontal scroll, so a long line is read by turning the wrap toggle on. Iced's scrollable
   owns one axis pair per box, not the two mirrored panes the reference composes; a shared horizontal
   scroll for a row pair would be a second layout model, so this is recorded rather than guessed at.

**Evidence and what it does not prove.** `shots/300-changes-split.png` (DP-2 alongside,
`status: passed`) shows the split layout: the hunk header across the row at the panel's inset, both
number gutters, the divider, red/green fills on their own sides and the clipped long line.
**Correction, round 506.** This section first claimed the split rows sat 23px apart where `CODE_LINE`
is 19, with an unexplained 4px per row, and that the row-by-row alignment was unverified. Measuring
the archived buffer line by line (`shots/300-changes-split.png`, ink bands at y 232/251/270/289) shows
rows exactly 19px apart, and the cropped frame reads line for line as the reference pairs them:
`11252|11252`, `11253-|11253+`, `empty|11254+`, `11254|11255`, `empty|11256+`. There was no 4px
defect; the claim came from eyeballing preview coordinates instead of measuring the buffer. The lesson
is the one this repository already states — measure the frame, do not read it off a scaled view. The
pairing test still pins the six rows, so neither the layout nor the pairing needs a follow-up.

**Mistakes inside this round.** The first capture drew the hunk header through the unified row view, so

`diff_split_full` replaced it. The first split row also had no divider, which the reference's

### Round 507 — a reminder popover with nothing left closes itself

**The gap.** Round 503's chip unmounts when the open session has no live reminder — the reference's
`ScheduleCatalogAction` returns `null` in the same case (`ScheduleCatalogAction.tsx:72-76`). But native
kept `reminders_open` set: after a deletion or a refresh that emptied the list, the popover disappeared
while its "open" flag survived, so the next successful read that added a reminder would **reopen a
popover the reader never asked for again**, with an armed delete row possibly still in it.

**The fix.** `close_spent_reminders` clears `reminders_open` and the armed row whenever the open
session has no live reminder; it runs after a catalog read settles (`Event::SchedulesLoaded`) and after
a successful delete (`Event::ScheduleDeleted`). The armed row goes with the popover for the same reason
round 503 gives when the popover is closed by hand: a confirmation must never be waiting for a row the
reader cannot see.

**Test.** `a_reminder_popover_closes_when_its_last_reminder_goes` — the `reminders` preset with an armed
delete, then a read that leaves only the other session's live reminder: the popover is closed, the
armed row is spent, and no entry is offered.

**Deliberately no capture.** The change removes state, not pixels: the frame after it is the ordinary
conversation with no chip, which `shots/297` already shows on the state side. A capture here would
prove nothing a suite assertion does not, so none was taken and the counter stays at 301. The rule
this respects is the one that matters — padding-only rounds need a frame; a state round needs the
assertion the frame cannot make.

### Round 510 — a settled row draws the flow margin, not a card's padding

**The gap.** Round 504 recorded it in its own words: "native still draws a 10px body
padding and flow gaps where the reference's spacing is entirely flow margins, so a
vertical comparison needs its own round." The 6/12 flow ladder had landed; the inner
padding had not. `chat_geometry::chrome_height` returned **32** for every message row —
16 above its body and 16 below — while the view drew only 10 of those
(`container(assembled).padding([10, 0])`), and the action row sat 6px under an assistant
body where the reference puts 16.

**The reference's model**, from its own sheets. `.scroll` pads 16px vertically and is the
transcript's only box (`ChatView.module.css:26-59`); a flow sibling's whole vertical box is
its `margin-top` — 6px, 12px around a response, 16px after a turn-process header
(`:60-95`). Assistant prose has no padding (`AssistantMarkdown.module.css:9-18`) and its
footer is `margin-top: 16px` under it (`:73-78`). The bubble is the one thing that pads its
own text, `10px 16px` (`.bubble`, `MessageItem.module.css:22-40`), with the actions a 6px
gap below it (`.userRow`, `:1-8`). `.actions` is 28px tall and centers its children
(`MessageIconActions.module.css:5-9`).

**What changed.** `chrome_height` is now the bubble's own 20px for a user row, nothing for
a settled assistant row, and the live/interrupted status block (24 + 7) on top of either;
`body_top` follows (10, 0, +31). `RESPONSE_ACTION_GAP` (16) joins `ACTION_GAP` (6) so
`action_footer` takes the row kind. The assistant container lost its box padding, a
file-only user row reserves no body and no chrome, and the action row centers its glyphs
and clocks. Because a settled message row no longer carries the 12px of symmetric chrome
that `row_geometries` swaps for the flow margin, `row_outer_chrome` now names the rows that
still do — tool lines, opaque records, command cards, expanded activity — so that
arithmetic is unchanged everywhere it still applies.

The arithmetic, per row: an assistant row is `body + 16 + 28` (was `body + 66`), a user row
is `20 + body + 6 + 28` (was `body + 60` reserved, `20 + body + 6 + 28` drawn).

**Measured, before → after, against `reference.png`** (`tool-activity`, both frames at
1980×1319; the reference is still a different state — cropped, scrolled, its own
conversation — so these are paired measurements, not a pixel diff):

| measure | reference | native before | native after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| tool-line pitch | 30 | 30 | **30** |
| bubble line pitch | 22 | 22 | **22** |
| last bubble ink → clock ink | 29 | 27 | 32 |
| clock + glyph ink band | 13 | 17 | **12** |
| last tool ink → next row's first ink | 26 (its tool → bubble) | 38 | **28** |
| assistant line pitch | 24 | 24 | **24** |

The clock moved 3px past the reference's offset (27 → 32 against 29) because the footer's
28px row now centers children as `.actions` does and DejaVu's `❐` has a taller ink box than
the web's icon; the band the eye reads (clock plus glyphs) went from 17 to 12 against 13.
That residue is the glyph, not the row, and the rule is now the reference's.

**A correction to how the reference frame was read.** Rounds 502, 504 and 509 described that
state as a "collapsed sidebar rail, no header". Measuring every band in the frame's left
520px found **no ink at all** (nothing above the background's luminance in any row), which

window: it starts left of the message column and below the header. Both the parity doc's

### Round 511 — a group seat belongs to its first row

**The gap, and how it was proved.** Round 510's note guessed that the 54px between the
fixture's Read and Edit lines came from "two seats for three calls". A temporary diagnostic
test over the same preset disproved that: the transcript has **one** seat with members
`[1, 2, 3]`. The real cause was a split ownership. `process_seat` was drawn as a sibling
*pushed before* its first member's row, while `row_geometries` reserved the seat's 24px line
*inside* that row — so an open group drew a header, then its first tool line, then a 24px
blank band where the reservation had no content. The projection also under-counted the drawn
Column by one seat line per group, and a **folded** group reserved nothing for the 24px seat
it draws.

**The reference makes the seat part of the group's one flow item.** `ChatGroupSeat.tsx:173-186`
renders one root holding the header div and the member body div; the collapsed root is
`height: calc(24px + var(--dsh-content-font-delta))` (`ChatGroupSeat.module.css:5-9`) and the
title button pads nothing (`:1-20`).

**The change.** `chat_geometry::seat_height(delta)` is the one value (`LINE_BODY + delta`)
the row reserves and the seat draws. The view pushes the seat into the first member's row box
instead of the Column, so header and member share one clipped, reserved box; a folded group
draws the same box shape holding only the seat (flow margin + 24px) and reserves exactly
that, while its hidden members reserve zero. The seat's own 6px/2px padding is gone, which is
how the header had grown taller than the line reserved for it.

**Measured** (`tool-activity`, 1980×1319, `shots/302-seat-in-row.png` against 301):

| measure | reference | before (301) | after (302) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first tool line → second tool line | 30 | 54 | **30** |
| seat header → its first tool line | — | 31 | **20** |
| every later tool line pitch | 30 | 30 | **30** |
| assistant first line after the last tool line | 26 (its tool → bubble) | 38 (ink) | 28 (ink) |

The folded state has its own frame: `shots/303-seat-folded.png` (`process-group-closed`,
1040×760) shows one header line, `▼ Read files, edited files, ran commands`, with no member
rows and the assistant paragraph correctly beneath it.

**Tests.** `a_group_seat_sits_inside_its_first_row_and_reserves_only_its_own_line` (renamed in round
512 to `a_group_seat_starts_folded_and_grows_by_its_title_gap_when_opened`, which keeps these
assertions and adds the fold) pins that
the row reserves the flow margin, one seat line and its own line — and that
`seat_height == LINE_BODY + delta`, so the drawn seat cannot outgrow its space.
`a_folded_group_reserves_the_seat_line_and_nothing_of_its_members` pins the folded
reservation. The *placement* is proven by the frame, not by the suite: Iced's test harness
sees no widget tree, which is exactly the class of failure this round fixed.

**Correction to round 510.** Its "the fixture's own group composition (two seats for three
calls) puts 54px between the Read and Edit lines" sentence was wrong twice — there is one
seat, and the 54px was this round's defect. The round-510 note now points here.

### Round 512 — a grouped seat is folded until the reader opens it

**The gap.** Native opened a live group's seat (`starts_folded(false) == false`, "a live turn's
group always starts open"). The reference does not: `ChatGroupSeat` owns a disclosure that begins
collapsed (`use-disclosure.ts`: "Own one initially collapsed disclosure") and hides the member body
whenever the group is grouped and unopened (`ChatGroupSeat.tsx:162`,
`useSearchableHidden(grouped && !open, …)`; the header stays). Since Standard is the desktop default
(`apply.ts:149`), the reference's running turn shows **one live line** — "Running commands · grep …" —
until the reader clicks it, where native showed every tool row.

**Two changes, because the click's default was the other half.** `starts_folded` is now
`fold_completed_turns && groups(settled)`, so every seat a mode draws starts folded.
`Message::ToggleProcessGroup` used `or_insert(true)` and flipped it — correct only while the default
was open; with a folded default the first click would have folded again. It now seeds `false` and
flips, so the first press opens the seat and the second closes it.

**The expanded title's gap.** An open seat's title takes `padding-bottom: 8px`
(`ChatGroupSeat.module.css:82-84`), which native had never drawn or reserved:
`chat_geometry::SEAT_TITLE_GAP` is that 8px, added to the first member's row when the seat is open
and drawn as a spacer between the header and the member. Measured at 1980×1319: the header's ink to
its first member's ink was **20px**, and is **28px** opened.

**A new preset, because the expanded state is now a click away.** `tool-activity-open` registers in
`PRESETS`, the size arm and the build (the `tool-activity` prefix already supplies its records) and
opens every seat the preset forms before the frame — the same class of state `process-group-closed`
already seeds.

**Frames.** `shots/304-seat-folded-live.png` (default Standard, `tool-activity`): the user bubble, the
clock, one `▼ Running commands · …` line, then the assistant answer — no tool rows. And
`shots/305-seat-opened.png` (`tool-activity-open`): the opened seat with its 8px title gap and the
three tool lines at the reference's 30px pitch.

**Correction to round 511's citation.** Round 511 wrote that the reference fixes the collapsed seat's
height with `.root:not([data-expanded]) { height: calc(24px + …) }` at
`ChatGroupSeat.module.css:5-9`. That rule is `ReasoningRow.module.css:6-9`, not the seat's. The seat's
header is a one-line title that pads nothing and inherits the body's type (`.title` at
`ChatGroupSeat.module.css:5-20`: `padding: 0`, `font: inherit`), which is why its height is the 24px
line — the value was right and the cited rule was wrong. The comment on
`chat_geometry::seat_height` says that instead.

**Tests.** `work_details::grouping_and_folding_follow_from_the_policy` now asserts a folded live
seat (and that Verbose folds neither state). The fixture's
`a_seat_click_folds_and_unfolds_its_members` asserts the flipped click order: folded at rest, open
after the first press, folded after the second. `a_group_seat_starts_folded_and_grows_by_its_title_gap_when_opened` replaces round 511's
open-by-default oracle: folded it reserves flow + the seat line;

### Round 518 — the turn rail marks every Turn the outline names

**The gap.** Round 517 built the ladder over the loaded window and named the missing half: the
reference merges that window with the `turnOutline` projection, so a Turn the window does not hold
keeps its mark — dimmed — and pressing it pages history to that Turn (`turn-rail-items.ts:72-89`).
Native had every projection in hand already: the snapshot's projection map is generic, and the
`turnOutline` wire view is the entries array (`session/session-turn-outline/src/projection.ts:61-137`:
`{turn, seq, prompt, response}`, strictly ascending, `turn/start` as the load-through seq).

**The change.** `turn_outline::turns` decodes that view, dropping an entry whose Turn or seq is
missing and an entry that would break the ascending order — the wire schema's own rules — so a damaged
projection states no marks rather than misplaced ones. `RailTurn` now carries a `RailAnchor`:
`Loaded(row)` scrolls to the Turn's first row, `Unloaded { seq }` pages history first. `rail_turns`
merges: every outline Turn gets a mark, loaded Turns keep their row anchor, and a loaded Turn the
(stale or absent) projection does not name still keeps its mark. `rail_press` states the decision in
one place — `Jump(row)`, `Page(turn)` while the window still has history, `Ignore` when it cannot
reach the Turn — and the update handler honours it: a jump clears any pending target, a page records
`rail_page_target` and asks for the page. `Event::Page` resumes a pending rail jump after every page:
jump when the Turn has arrived, ask for the next page while history remains, forget the target when
neither holds (`TurnNavigator.tsx:98-108`). The ladder draws an unloaded mark at 40% length, the
reference's `markUnloaded` (`TurnNavigator.module.css:85-88`).

The paging request itself was factored into `App::load_older`, now shared by the `Load earlier` control
and the rail, so there is one page request path.

**Fixture.** `turn-rail` now states the rail's real shape: the window holds the newest four Turns
(5–8) and the seeded outline names all eight, so turns 1–4 are the unloaded marks. Two fixture
invariants had to move with it: the snapshot's `cursor` is now read from the last record's `seq`
instead of `len - 1` (a window that starts mid-session must state its own newest seq), and `hasMore`
is true for this preset so the paging path is reachable.

**Frame.** `shots/313-rail-outline.png` (1400x820): eight ticks — four short dim ones for the outline's
older Turns, the active fifth Turn full length in primary ink, and three more loaded marks below.

descending Turn with the good entry after them kept; absent/malformed → none), plus
`the_turn_rail_marks_each_loaded_turn_once_at_its_first_row` (eight marks, 1–4 unloaded at seqs 0/3/6/9,
5–8 loaded at rows 0/2/4/6), `a_press_on_an_unloaded_rail_mark_pages_history_towards_its_turn`

### Round 520 — a paging rail mark breathes, and a long ladder shows a window

**The gap.** Round 519's handover named the last two drawing differences in the rail: the reference
pulses the mark whose Turn is still being paged, and it scrolls a ladder taller than its 420px band
with faded ends (`TurnNavigator.module.css:52-95,95-99,186-193`).

**The pulse.** `App.rail_pulse` is a ten-step phase; a `Message::RailPulseTick` subscription runs only
while `rail_page_target` is set, one step per 100ms, so the reference's one-second cycle divides into
ten. `rail_mark_alpha(phase)` is the reference's `dsh-turn-mark-busy` keyframes as a triangle — full at
the ends, **0.35** in the middle — and the paging mark's ink takes that alpha. Measured in the frame:
the busy tick's peak luminance is 141 against its neighbours' 207, and the active mark reads 690 and
the hovered one 454, so the three states are distinguishable in one picture.

**The window.** The reference scrolls the ladder inside its frame behind 24px mask fades. Iced has no
mask, so native shows the same band as a **window**: `rail_window(len, focus)` returns at most 42 marks
(the 420px band over the 10px pitch) around the Turn the viewport is in, clamped to either end of the
ladder. A long session therefore keeps every mark reachable instead of clipping the ones past 42 —
the reference's fades are named as the difference, not the reachability.

**Frame.** `shots/315-rail-busy.png` (1400x820): the `turn-rail-hover` preset now also seeds a paging
target on the second Turn and the pulse at its dip, so one frame shows the card beside the sixth mark,
the active fifth mark at full length, and the second mark dimmed mid-pulse.

**Tests.** `a_paging_mark_breathes_from_full_to_a_third_at_the_reference_cycle` (full at 0, 0.35 at the
midpoint, the phase wraps, falling then rising through the halves, ten steps per second) and
`a_long_ladder_shows_a_window_around_the_turn_in_view` (a short ladder draws every mark; a long one
keeps 42 around its focus without running past either end; no focus falls back to the head).

**Recording honesty.** A still frame cannot prove an *animation*: it proves the states the animation
moves through. The pulse's timing rests on the tick's 100ms period and the phase arithmetic the test
pins, not on the capture.

### Round 525 — a workflow run that lost its process reads as interrupted

**The gap.** The coverage table recorded the workflow-run surface as cloned "no interrupted
detection". The reference has five run states, not three: `running | completed | failed | cancelled |
interrupted`, and it derives the last one without any extra event — a run whose `stopReason` is absent
while its enclosing step or turn is **closed** was interrupted, and every member of such a run that
never reported an outcome is interrupted too (`workflow-definition.ts:87-124`). Native drew
`running` for every stoppless run, so a run whose process died claimed to be alive forever.

**The change.** `workflow_run_status(stop, turn_closed)` is the reference's rule as a pure function;
`Transcript::turn_at(seq)` finds the turn that was open at a log position, because a `tool-workflow/*`
record carries no turn of its own; and the card marks the run `Interrupted` in muted ink with a `◌`
member glyph where a stoppless member used to show the running dot. A run inside a turn that has not
ended still says `running`, which is the honest state for the live case.

**Frame.** `shots/319-workflow-interrupted.png` (760x560, new `workflow-run-interrupted` preset: a run
that started, reported two members, never stopped, inside a closed turn):
`Workflow PUBLIC interrupted workflow … Interrupted`, then `Phase · research` and `Phase · write`, each
member on `◌`.

**Tests.** `a_workflow_run_without_a_stop_reason_is_interrupted_once_its_turn_closed` (every stop
reason still wins; a stoppless run is `running` while its turn is open and `Interrupted` once it
closes) and `the_turn_at_a_workflow_runs_start_decides_whether_it_closed` (a real snapshot folds the
run, `turn_at` finds turn 1, `turn_ended` is true, and the status follows).

**Recorded limit.** The reference also treats a closed *step* as enough to interrupt a run. Native
reads only the turn, which is the conservative direction: a run inside a still-open turn keeps saying
`running` even if its step closed, so native never claims an interruption that the record does not
support.

### Round 526 — a Turn's usage is the sum of its attempts

**The gap.** Rounds 521 read one assistant record's `usage`. The reference never does: its disclosure
is "exact provider-reported token accounting for **every attempt in one completed Turn**"
(`contract/chat-nodes.ts:68-83`), folded by `deriveTurnTokenUsage` from `turn/start` through
`turn/end` (`packages/llm/token-meter/src/turn-usage.ts:126-300`). A Turn that retried therefore
reported only its last attempt in native, and a Turn with several steps showed one pill per assistant
row instead of one pill per Turn.

**The change.** New `app/src/turn_usage.rs` is that fold: a three-state attempt machine (pending /
open / settled) over the Turn's own records, one sample per attempt boundary
(`step/start`, `llm/retry-started` → open; `assistant/attempt`/`assistant/message` → a sample;
`step/end`, `llm/retry` → idle), usage read from `data.usage` **or** the stream's last usage chunk, the
route read from the message's own `source`, safe sums, and the reference's bucket rule — `cacheRead` /
`cacheWrite` / `reasoning` survive only when **every** attempt reported them, routes only when every
attempt named one. Any missing boundary, unbracketed Turn, attempt without usage or contradictory step
end makes the whole disclosure unavailable, and the caller keeps the single-record reading it had.

`Transcript::turn_usage`/`turn_usage_detail` now prefer the aggregate and only on the assistant record
that **closes** the Turn, so the pill appears once per Turn.

**Frame.** `shots/320-turn-usage-retry.png` (1040x760, new `turn-usage-retry` preset: two attempts with
a retry between them): one `Usage 3.0K tok` pill and a dialog reading `Turn usage 3.0K tok`,
`Provider / model PUBLIC/PUBLIC-model`, `Cache hit 90.0%`, `Uncached input 300 tok`,
`Cached input 2.7K tok`, `Output 30 tok` — the sum of 1010 and 2020, not the 2020 the last message
alone reported.

**Tests.** Six in `turn_usage`: two closed attempts summed (and a second sample in one step refused);
an unbracketed Turn, an unclosed attempt and an attempt without usage each yield `None`; and cache
buckets/routes surviving only with unanimous reports (including route deduplication).

**Recorded limits.** Native's fold accepts a sample from `data.usage` or the stream's last usage chunk
where the reference also accepts `streamUsage` on attempt records; native treats `llm/retry` as
closing a settled attempt, which is the reference's own step-end path. The aggregate is not a Host
projection — it is derived from the same retained records in both clients.

### Round 528 — raw HTML stays literal instead of failing the whole reply

**The gap.** The reference runs no HTML parser: a `html` node's `value` is returned as literal text, so
`<b>` on screen is the four characters `<b>` and the markdown around it still formats
(`ui-primitives/src/markdown/render.tsx:333-335`). Native refused `Event::Html`/`InlineHtml`, and a
refusal fails the **whole document** — so one `<br>` or `<div align="center">` in a reply dropped every
heading, table and code block to plain text.

**The change.** Both events are drawn as literal text; a block-level fragment opens the paragraph it
will sit in and keeps its trailing line break out of the text, and `TagEnd::HtmlBlock` closes that
paragraph so the next block does not inherit it. `Tag::HtmlBlock`/`TagEnd::HtmlBlock` are now named
containers. With every `Event` variant handled, the catch-all arm is gone and the match is exhaustive,
so a parser upgrade that adds a variant fails to compile instead of landing in an opaque refusal —
that removed the round's one new warning.

**Frame.** `shots/322-markdown-html.png` (1040x760, new `markdown-html` preset, recaptured from the
binary built after the exhaustive-match change): `PUBLIC text before <b>markup</b> and after.`, then the
literal block `<div align="center">PUBLIC literal block</div>` on its own line, then
`**Markdown still formats** in this paragraph.` drawn bold — three behaviours in one frame: inline
markup kept literal, a block fragment kept literal, and the surrounding markdown still formatted.

**Tests.** `raw_html_stays_literal_text_in_the_flow` (inline and block fragments keep their characters,
no span is treated as markup, and a block fragment becomes its own paragraph); the unsupported lists
that used HTML now use a titled image and a titled link, which stay refused;
`unsupported_document_preserves_complete_source_and_nonce_exhaustion_disables_actions` and the search
test gained a titled image as their inert-markup case.

**Recorded difference.** The reference's literal HTML text sits in an HTML flow where whitespace
collapses; native draws the same characters in a paragraph whose newlines are line breaks, so a

### Round 530 — a quote and a list compose instead of failing the reply

**The gap.** The last structural refusal from round 529: `> - item` (a list inside a quote) and `- > item`
(a quote inside a list item) failed the whole document, because the flat paragraph model stored list
depth and quote membership in separate fields and could not say which container opened first — the
reference nests them in DOM order (`ui-primitives/src/markdown/render.tsx:281-289,425-460`).

**The change.** The builder keeps a small container stack and records one bit on each paragraph:
`quote_first`, true when the quote opened before any list. The renderer draws the rule on the outside of
the indents in that case and after the item's own marker otherwise — so `> - item` renders rule, indent,
bullet, text and `- > item` renders bullet, rule, text, exactly the two nestings the reference draws.
Both refusals are gone. A quoting paragraph still measures the same total inset, so heights are
unchanged; `Block::Paragraph` patterns elsewhere ignore the new field with `..`.

over `> - quoted list item` / `> - second item` (rule outside, bullet inside), then

eight mixed sources failed, and now asserts four of them keep their order, a third nested level still
draws, and a preceding valid block no longer poisons the source. The "inert markup" exemplars across

**Recorded limits.** One bit cannot express more than two mixed containers: `> - > item` collapses to

### Round 531 — two quoted paragraphs share one rule

**The gap round 530 recorded.** Native drew one bar per quoted paragraph, each starting *below* its own
16px top margin, so a two-paragraph quote showed a notch between the bars where the reference's one
`<blockquote>` has a single continuous `border-left` across all its children
(`ui-primitives/src/markdown/MarkdownText.module.css:151-156`, `render.tsx:281-289`).

**The change.** `continues_quote(blocks, index)` decides when a quoted paragraph continues the rule
opened before it — the previous block must be a quoted paragraph with the same container order and
indent. For a continuation the paragraph draws its rule *taller* by its own top margin and moves its
text down by that margin inside the rule, and the wrapper's leading gap becomes zero: the element's
total height is unchanged, so no measurement moved, but the margin now sits inside the bar. The first
quoted paragraph keeps its margin outside, which is the reference's `blockquote { margin: 16px 0 0 }`.

**The frame caught a real defect first.** The first capture showed the second paragraph clipped to a
sliver: the wrapper still reserved only `block_height + gap` while the content had grown by the covered
margin. The wrapper now adds `gap + covered`, and the recapture shows both paragraphs whole.

the committed source: "Before the quote.", then one bar beside a two-line first paragraph and a second
paragraph — no notch — then "After the quote." back at the left edge. The zoomed crop used to check the
join shows the bar unbroken.

**Tests.** `only_a_matching_quoted_paragraph_continues_the_rule` (a plain paragraph opens the rule, a
matching quoted one continues it, a plain successor does not, a different container order or indent is
a different blockquote, and index 0 has no predecessor).
